content.description: In 1953, Watson and Crick described the double helix of DNA. Behind that glory stands the crucial work of Rosalind Franklin.

hero.hook: The shape of a molecule, and the secret of heredity.

blocks.text: People knew that traits pass from parents to children. But what chemical object carries the information? In the middle of the 20th century, the answer came into focus: **DNA**.
In **1953**, **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** published a famous model, the **double helix**. That shape explains how DNA can copy itself.
DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is a long molecule found in our cells. It holds chemical “letters” that spell out a code. But in the 1940s and 1950s, its shape in three dimensions was still unknown.
Without the shape, it was hard to see how that code could duplicate itself at every cell division.
**Rosalind Franklin**, a physicist and chemist, obtained images of DNA using X-rays. Her famous **Photo 51** showed clear signs of a helix.
Watson and Crick saw her data, in circumstances now judged unfair to Franklin, and built their model. Franklin died in 1958. The 1962 Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins, not to her.
Franklin also did major work on viruses. Her part in the DNA story was underrated for a long time in popular accounts.

blocks.caption: Two complementary strands: copying suddenly becomes imaginable

blocks.text: Two strands wind around each other. The letters face one another in pairs. When the strands come apart, each one can serve as a template to rebuild the other. Heredity became a chemical mechanism you could actually picture.
Out of this discovery came modern genetics, sequencing, DNA tests, and gene therapy. And ethical debates too: what should we do with that power?
In **1953**, the double helix model explained how DNA stores and copies the information of life. Franklin supplied decisive evidence that was erased from the story for far too long.

DNA replication.explanation: The process by which the double helix unwinds and each strand serves as a template for the synthesis of a complementary strand. This mechanism ensures the faithful transmission of genetic information during each cell division.

Friedrich Miescher.explanation: Swiss biologist who first isolated a substance he called "nuclein" (DNA) in the nuclei of white blood cells in 1869.

Linus Pauling.explanation: Genius American chemist, rival to Watson and Crick, who mistakenly proposed a triple helix structure for DNA shortly before 1953.

Rosalind Franklin.explanation: A crystallographer whose Photo 51 (an X-ray diffraction image of DNA) was passed to Watson and Crick without her consent. She had understood the helical structure, but the data was "borrowed" from her. Having died in 1958, she could not receive the 1962 Nobel Prize.

X-ray crystallography.explanation: Analytical technique used to determine the atomic structure of a crystal by observing how it deflects a beam of X-rays.

genome sequencing.explanation: Method used to determine the precise order of nitrogenous bases (A, T, C, G) all along a DNA molecule.
